chapters.name: Chapter 1: AI as a STEM tool

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Problem sets with verified solutions
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Generate STEM practice with AI and verify every solution.
This lesson builds toward: Given AI-made STEM practice problems with solutions, you will check every solution with a second method, a calculator or a graphing tool, before students see any problem.
AI can produce many practice problems fast: word problems with real-world contexts, problems at several difficulty levels, and step-by-step worked solutions. That saves time, but AI is known to make arithmetic and reasoning errors, especially in multi-step problems, and can state a wrong answer confidently.
So verify every solution. Work it yourself, check it with a calculator or graphing tool such as Desmos, or ask the AI to check its answer by a second method and compare. If the two methods disagree, work it out yourself.
Ask for problems with clean numbers for practice, or realistic messy numbers for application. Ask for common mistakes students make on each problem; those make good discussion questions.
Step by step:
- Ask for problems at the level and context you need.
- Ask for step-by-step solutions.
- Work or check every answer with a calculator or graphing tool.
- Ask for a second method and compare.
- Ask for common mistakes to discuss.
Words to know:
- Worked solution: a solution showing every step.
- Verify: check that something is correct using another method or source.
Try it now: Ask AI for six multi-step problems on a topic you teach, with solutions. Verify each one and count how many were wrong.
You can now generate STEM practice with AI and verify every solution before students see it.

check.q: Where is AI especially likely to make mistakes in math?
check.why: AI makes arithmetic and reasoning errors, especially across several steps.

check.q: AI's worked solution and your calculator check give different answers. What would you do?
options: Trust the AI because it showed steps
check.why: When two methods disagree, the lesson says to work it out yourself.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Data investigations with AI as a coding helper
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Plan a data investigation where AI helps write code students check and explain.
This lesson builds toward: Given a public dataset and an AI coding helper, you will plan a data investigation where students comment each line of code, predict the result and check one number by hand, with every understanding step included.
Real data makes STEM real. Students can investigate public datasets (weather, health, sports, environment) in Google Colab, a free Python notebook in the browser; it needs a Google account, and free resources are not guaranteed, so save work often. Check your district's rules for student Google accounts first.
AI can be a coding helper: students describe what they want ("read this CSV and make a line graph of temperature by month") and AI suggests code. Many students can then run code they could not yet write alone, and learn from it.
Build in understanding: students must add a comment to each line explaining what it does, predict the graph before running the code, and check one number in the output by hand. If they cannot explain the code, they have not learned it yet.
Step by step:
- Choose a public dataset and a question.
- Students ask AI to help write code for one step.
- Students comment each line in their own words.
- Predict the result, then run the code.
- Check one number by hand.
Words to know:
- Dataset: an organized collection of data, often a table.
- CSV: a simple file format for tables, with values separated by commas.
- Code comment: a note in code, often starting with #, that explains what the code does.
Official sources:
- Google Colab FAQ
Try it now: Find a public dataset on a topic your students care about. Use AI to help write code in Colab that graphs one variable, add a comment to every line, and check one number by hand.
You can now plan a data investigation where AI helps with code and students show understanding.

options: A free Python notebook that runs in the browser
A tool that only makes slides
check.why: Colab lets students run Python in a browser with a Google account.

check.q: A student ran AI-written code and got a graph but cannot say what the code does. What would you do?
options: Have them comment each line in their own words and check one number by hand
Ask AI to write a longer program
Give them a lower grade and move on
check.why: If students cannot explain the code, they have not learned it yet.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Simulations, visuals and explanations
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to create explanations and visuals, and check them for misconceptions.
This lesson builds toward: Given an AI explanation, analogy or diagram, you will find and fix misconceptions by checking it against your curriculum or a trusted source, before using it in class.
AI can explain STEM ideas in several ways (an analogy, a step-by-step, a story) and suggest diagrams, simulations or demonstrations. Free simulation and graphing tools such as PhET simulations and Desmos let students explore; AI can help you write the guiding questions.
Watch for misconceptions. AI analogies can mislead (for example, explaining electric current with water flow in ways that break down), and AI-generated diagrams can be scientifically wrong. Check every explanation against your curriculum and a trusted source.
A useful classroom move: give students an AI explanation with a deliberate or real error and ask them to find and fix it. Finding errors in AI output is a scientific skill.
Step by step:
- Ask AI for two or three explanations of a concept.
- Check each against your curriculum and a trusted source.
- Use AI to write guiding questions for a simulation.
- Check diagrams for scientific accuracy.
- Have students find errors in an AI explanation.
Words to know:
- Simulation: a computer model that lets you explore how something works.
- Analogy: explaining something by comparing it to something familiar.
- Misconception: a common wrong idea about how something works.
Try it now: Ask AI to explain one STEM concept you teach in two different ways. Find any misconception in each, and write a find-the-error task for students.
You can now use AI explanations and simulations while catching their misconceptions.

check.q: What is the risk of an AI analogy in science?
options: It can mislead where the analogy breaks down
check.why: Analogies like water for electric current can break down and create misconceptions.

check.q: An AI-made diagram you plan to show looks wrong in one place. What would you do?
options: Check it against your curriculum or a trusted source and fix it
Show it anyway because AI made it
Delete every AI diagram you have
check.why: AI diagrams can be scientifically wrong, so check them before use.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: AI as a STEM subject

lessons.title: Lesson 4: How machines learn from data
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Teach the basic idea of machine learning with a hands-on example.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free tool or an unplugged card activity, you will explain how machine learning uses training data to make predictions and why varied data matters, with a working classroom example.
Machine learning is a STEM topic students can understand. The core idea: instead of writing rules, we show a program many labeled examples (training data) and it finds patterns, then makes predictions on new examples. Its accuracy depends on the data: too few examples, or examples that are not varied, lead to wrong predictions.
Hands-on: free tools such as Google's Teachable Machine let students train a simple image or sound classifier in a browser; check its terms and your district's approval before student use. An unplugged version works too: students sort cards of animals by features and write rules, then test on new cards.
Then ask the big questions: What happens if training data only shows one kind of example? How would we measure accuracy? This links machine learning to statistics, data quality and fairness.
Step by step:
- Explain: labeled examples in, patterns found, predictions out.
- Train a simple classifier, or do the unplugged card sort.
- Test it on new examples.
- Change the training data and see what happens.
- Discuss accuracy, data quality and fairness.
Words to know:
- Machine learning: programs that learn patterns from examples instead of following hand-written rules.
- Training data: the labeled examples a program learns from.
- Classifier: a program that sorts things into categories.
Try it now: Plan a 20-minute activity where students train (or simulate, unplugged) a simple classifier, then change the training data and explain what happened to its predictions.
You can now teach the core idea of machine learning with a hands-on activity.

check.q: What is the core idea of machine learning?
options: A person writes every rule by hand
A program finds patterns in many labeled examples
check.why: Machine learning learns from training data instead of hand-written rules.

check.q: Your class has no devices for Teachable Machine. What would you do?
options: Run the unplugged version: sort animal cards by features, write rules, test on new cards
check.why: The unplugged card activity teaches the same idea without devices.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Verifying AI claims like a scientist
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Teach students a routine to test AI claims against evidence.
This lesson builds toward: Given an AI claim such as a statistic, conversion or citation, you will apply the claim, evidence, test, conclude routine, reaching accept, reject or not enough evidence with a reason.
Scientific thinking is the best defense against AI errors. Teach a four-step routine: Claim: what exactly does the AI say? Evidence: what data or source would show it is true? Test: check the claim against data, a calculation, an experiment or a trusted source. Conclude: accept, reject or "not enough evidence".
Practice with STEM claims AI might get wrong: a unit conversion, a statistic, a cause-and-effect claim, a chemical formula, or a citation that may not exist. Students learn that AI sources must be found and checked, not trusted.
This routine works across subjects and builds the habit you want for life: AI output is a hypothesis to test, not an answer to copy.
Step by step:
- Claim: state exactly what AI says.
- Evidence: what would show it is true?
- Test: data, calculation, experiment or trusted source.
- Conclude: accept, reject or not enough evidence.
Words to know:
- Claim: a statement that something is true.
- Hypothesis: an idea that can be tested.
- Citation: a reference to a source of information.
Try it now: Collect three STEM claims from an AI tool on a topic you teach. Run each through the four-step routine and note which held up.
You can now teach students to test AI claims like scientists.

check.q: In the verification routine, what comes right after "Claim"?
check.why: The routine is Claim, Evidence, Test, Conclude.

check.q: AI gives students a statistic with a citation. What should they do?
options: Copy the citation into their report
Ask AI if the citation is real
Find the source and check it exists and says that
check.why: AI sources must be found and checked, not trusted.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Engineering design and tasks that show reasoning
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Use AI in the engineering design process and design tasks where reasoning stays visible.
This lesson builds toward: When planning a STEM task or design challenge, you will design a task where students show their own reasoning and label its AI use level, with a verification step and an explanation in students' own words.
In the engineering design process (define the problem, brainstorm, plan, build, test, improve), AI is most useful at the brainstorming and improving stages: generating many design ideas, suggesting tests, or explaining why a prototype failed. Students still choose, build, test and justify.
Because AI can solve many textbook problems, design tasks where reasoning is visible: ask students to explain why a method works, compare two methods, find an error, make a prediction before calculating, or apply the idea to their own data or design. Oral explanations and lab notebooks show thinking.
Label each task with an AI use level so students know when AI is a tool and when the skill must be shown alone, and explain why.
Step by step:
- Use AI for brainstorming and improving in design.
- Students choose, build, test and justify.
- Design tasks: explain, compare, find errors, predict, apply.
- Use oral explanations and lab notebooks.
- Label the AI use level for each task.
Words to know:
- Engineering design process: the cycle of defining a problem, designing, building, testing and improving.
- Prototype: an early model built to test an idea.
- Lab notebook: a record of what a student did, observed and concluded.
Try it now: Final task: plan your STEM lesson where students use an approved AI tool in an investigation or design challenge, with a verification step, a reasoning task in their own words, and an AI use level. Teach it if you can and note what students found when they checked the AI.
You can now lead STEM learning where students use AI as a tool, check it rigorously and keep their own reasoning visible.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds AI as a tool in an investigation AI does the investigation for students, or the tool is not approved. Students use an approved AI tool for one clear part, such as writing code or brainstorming designs. Students also predict what the AI's output should show before they run it. Verification step No step where students check the AI's output. Students check the AI's code, numbers or claims against data, a calculation or a test. Students record a conclusion: accept, reject or not enough evidence, with a reason. Reasoning in their own words Students only hand in an answer or a graph. A task where students explain their reasoning in their own words. Students also compare two methods or find an error. AI use level No AI use level is given. The task is labeled with an AI use level. The plan explains to students why that level fits the task. Teacher checked the materials AI-made problems, code or explanations were not checked. Every AI-made solution and explanation was checked before class. The plan names the method used to check, such as a calculator, Desmos or a trusted source. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: At which stages of the engineering design process is AI most useful?
check.why: AI helps generate ideas and explain failures; students still choose, build, test and justify.

check.q: AI can solve your textbook problem set. What would you change so reasoning stays visible?
options: Assign more of the same problems
Ask students to predict first and explain why the method works
check.why: Predicting, explaining and comparing methods show thinking that AI cannot do for them.
